prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which opened a new regime of precision measurement of time

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a measurement advance that changed what can be measured. The magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while thousands of atoms are interrogated at once, so statistics and systematics improve together and fractional uncertainty reaches about 1e-18. That is a figure of merit I trust because independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL) reproduce it and compare clocks directly, including over optical fibre links. Six of eight members ranked it, three of them first, and the arguments differ in kind (instrument, tests of fundamental physics, geodesy), which suggests the support is not just agreement on a label. The credit is also the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori made the concept and the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye's group brought it to the accuracy and stability frontier, so a two-person prize needs no arbitrary cut. The impact is arriving now through relativistic geodesy at the centimetre scale, tests of constant variation, dark-matter searches and the pending redefinition of the second.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that this is a continuation of the 2005 frequency-comb prize (Hall, Hansch) and the 2012 prize for single-ion control (Wineland), and that a committee could call it an instrument refinement, not a discovery. Others who shaped the field (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto, Ovsiannikov) are outside the credited names, and Ye's reputation also rests on comb-based spectroscopy. I think the citation can answer this by rewarding the lattice concept and its realisation, not clocks in general. But I admit that the 2005 and 2012 prizes are the same adjacent ground, and that some colleagues may weigh that more heavily than I do.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first and sees it as a clean fundamental advance, with Katori and Ye as a fair pair. She also notes that Ludlow, Ovsiannikov and Takamoto are not credited, and that the 2005 and 2012 prizes might make it look incremental to some.
responses.response: I agree on the pair and on the independent-laboratory evidence. I would go a step further on credit: Takamoto's 2005 Nature demonstration is part of Katori's group's work, so it is largely covered by Katori's name. I also disagree with her ranking of B047 second and B033 only seventh. For me the gap is smaller, because trapped-ion gates have measured fidelities and coherence times that I trust. Her point that Wineland already covered ion control is fair for B033, but then B022 has the same exposure, so it cannot be used against only one.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks baryon acoustic oscillations first as a clean discovery from nature that turned dark energy into a measured expansion history. He worries about repeated cosmology prizes and about credit across SDSS, 2dFGRS and theory predecessors.
responses.response: I take the force of this. BAO is an elegant standard ruler and the DESI results make it topical. My reservation is attribution. Two survey collaborations of hundreds of people detected the peak in the same year, and the idea predates both in work by Peebles, Yu, Sunyaev and Zeldovich. Three names then represent a collective detection quite loosely. The lattice clock has a sharper line from invention to realisation, and a measurement that is reproduced by independent clocks is, I think, a firmer basis than a peak seen once in two surveys. I do not rank BAO low, but I would want the committee to settle who the discoverers are before it can be preferred.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube first as an instrument-driven discovery that created neutrino astronomy, and ranks the lattice clock second as a measurement-technology advance of the first rank. He is unsure whether the leadership credit can be separated from a roughly 300-person collaboration.
responses.response: We share the instrument-driven criterion, and that is why I think his top two are close. Where we differ is attribution. IceCube is a very large collaboration with AMANDA and DUMAND precursors, and I cannot see how two names capture it without ignoring most of the people whose calibration and background rejection made the result. With the lattice clock the credited people are the ones who made it work. I would like to hear what evidence he would use to separate Halzen's and Karle's role, because without that I cannot place B046 above B022.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and presents it as a natural complement to the 2025 circuit prize, with the transmon-era architecture used in nearly all superconducting processors. He declares that he works in the field.
responses.response: I agree that cQED is real and widely used, and I ranked it fourth. My difficulty is timing and attribution. The 2025 prize covers the superconducting-circuit lineage, and I would struggle to explain to outsiders why this second prize in the field is a different discovery. Koch, Schoelkopf and others invented the transmon, and Girvin and Devoret were part of the 2004 proposal, so Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf is not a clean trio. Given his stated conflict, I think his first place should count with some discount, and I would keep B039 as a later candidate.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which depends on how the citation is framed.
How much credit belongs to other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto) that cannot be named under the two-name configuration.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the redefinition of the second, which would make the practical impact explicit but is not needed for the scientific case.
My knowledge of the exact priority dates for the magic-wavelength proposal and the first demonstrations is from memory and has not been checked.
statement.conflict_note: Specific connections from my profile: I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory during my PhD, and Hall (2005 laureate) worked closely with the JILA group in which Jun Ye is active, so I have a scientific proximity to the JILA environment, though no co-authorship or collaboration with Ye or Katori is recorded in my profile. I also lead quantum sensing in WACQT and run a company on slow-light filters, both of which give me interest in precision measurement as such. This may warrant a mention to the chair, but I do not think it requires recusal. No other specific conflict is apparent from the profile for B033, B047 or the other shortlisted candidates.
